articles.title: Connective Resource Mobilization: A Relational Approach to Movement Continuity in Transnational Activism
articles.abstract: Social movement studies have long centered social movement organizations (SMOs) as the primary vehicles of mobilization. Yet contemporary movements are increasingly decentralized and digitally mediated, challenging SMO-centric frameworks such as resource mobilization theory (RMT). As contention becomes more individualized and non-conventional, organization- and event-centered approaches struggle to explain how movements persist, evolve, or dissolve under shifting conditions. Drawing on RMT and economic sociology, this article advances a relational resource mobilization framework through four propositions: resource mobilization (1) is historically contingent; (2) translates into tactics differently across organizational configurations; (3) is relational; and (4) provides an analytic for examining movement continuity across time and space. Within this framework, I introduce the model of connective resource mobilization to theorize how digitally mediated movements generate strategic capacity through personalized earmarking practices across borders and phases of contention. Based on 179 interviews and observation at 187 events in Hong Kong and Canada, I trace how the Hong Kong Pro-Democracy Movement evolved from its 2019 protest peak through its subsequent downturn across domestic and diasporic contexts. The analysis demonstrates how a relational approach to resource mobilization can illuminate divergent trajectories of movement continuity across historical, geographic, political, and socio-technological contexts.

articles.title: On legacy persistence: historical KKK organizations and racial exclusion in American sundown towns
articles.authors: Kunyuan Qiao, Ashley V Reichelmann, Matthew O Hunt
articles.abstract: Why do some communities perpetuate historical patterns of racial exclusion while others abandon them? We examine American sundown towns, communities that from the 1890s through the 1960s barred people of color from remaining within their borders after sunset. We argue that Second Wave Ku Klux Klan (KKK) organizations, active from 1915 through the 1940s, institutionalized and enforced this exclusion, embedding it in local structures. These structures imprinted White adolescents with negative racial attitudes toward Black people, and imprinted individuals subsequently engaged in residential sorting, remaining in or relocating to sundown towns with a strong KKK presence while avoiding those without such a history. Second Wave Klan prevalence therefore predicts the racial attitudes of White residents in historical sundown towns today. We find support for our hypotheses in a sample of more than 600 White respondents surveyed in historical sundown towns. We advance research on place-based racial legacies by showing that historical organized enforcement helps explain why legacies persist unevenly across communities and that this persistence operates through two individual-level mechanisms: attitudinal imprinting and residential sorting.

articles.title: Review of “Island Time: Theory Groups and the Social Production of Scientific Knowledge”
Generational imprinting: how political events shape cohorts
articles.abstract: Contemporary narratives of generational politics propose that formative experiences produce shared political opinions across an age cohort. In this article, I advance a theory of cohortization to challenge that view, arguing that large–scale political events produce differentiation within cohorts as much as differentiation between them. I investigate the implications of this framework through the killing of George Floyd and the subsequent Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, analyzing attitudes toward law enforcement among non-Hispanic White Americans from 2016 to 2024. Using survey data from Cooperative Congressional Election Study, American National Election Study, and the Nationscape, I show that younger and older cohorts diverged after the event, but this differentiation was driven exclusively by young Democrats and Independents. The end result was not a unified generation, but one internally divided along party lines. This finding qualifies theories of generational politics, emphasizing that formative experiences may intensify existing political divisions within cohorts.

articles.title: Life and debt in rural America
articles.abstract: Sociology’s growing focus on household debt and wealth has overlooked a potentially salient axis of inequality: rural–urban disparities in the United States. Key facets of rural life indicate a disadvantage (e.g., higher poverty rates, lack of mainstream financial institutions) and a simultaneous advantage (e.g., predominantly White populations, lower cost of living). To address evidence gaps on rural–urban disparities in debt and wealth, we use Consumer Expenditure Survey data to (1) estimate rural–urban disparities in multiple kinds of household debt and wealth, (2) examine what may be driving these disparities, and (3) assess whether these disparities also vary by race. Our findings show that place is an important axis of US financial inequality. Compared to urban households, rural households consistently have less credit card, student loan, and mortgage principal debt, but they also have less retirement and liquid savings, and their homes are worth less. These differences largely persist above controls, suggesting that rurality shapes financial outcomes in ways not fully explained by income dynamics and population composition. Racial variations in debt and wealth are also pronounced within rural areas, mirroring national patterns. We offer careful interpretations of our findings in order to gauge the financial and material wellbeing of rural households, which is needed in a time of growing rural–urban economic and social divides.

The Cognitive Housework Inventory: Developing Survey Questions to Measure the Division of Cognitive Housework
articles.abstract: Housework is unequally shared in different-gender couples, leading to negative consequences for women and lowering couples’ relationship quality. Although qualitative research identifies cognitive housework as an important type of household labor, we lack validated measures of cognitive housework to use in survey settings, barring quantitative research on its division in broader populations and its effects on household members. We use an open-ended survey and cognitive interviews to develop the Cognitive Housework Inventory (CHI), a seven-item survey instrument to measure the division of cognitive housework among partnered individuals. We then validate the CHI using data from an online survey, along with pairwise correlations, exploratory factor analysis, and bivariate analyses by gender. Regression analyses estimating its associations with stress, burnout, and relationship satisfaction demonstrate how to use the CHI in empirical settings. Results indicate the CHI is a valid and parsimonious instrument that can be incorporated into larger surveys to ultimately generate additional quantitative data on the distribution of housework.

articles.title: A Replication Framework for Observational Research: From Specification Restriction to Specification Expansion
articles.authors: Jonathan Ben-Menachem, Ari Galper, Nic Fishman
articles.abstract: Sociology has remained relatively insulated from debates about the “replication crisis.” Heeding calls to consider replication more deeply, we introduce a distinction between two types of research reforms that have emerged in the wake of the crisis: specification-restricting and specification-expanding reforms. Specification restriction is often promoted as a way to increase the repeatability of research findings by controlling false positives. We argue that this statistical justification is less compelling in observational contexts—where the assumptions licensing false-positive control are harder to sustain and rigid ex ante analytical commitments can instead enshrine fragile specifications—than in experimental contexts. We further argue that apparently low replication rates do not necessarily imply a high prevalence of false positive findings. Instead, we propose a replication framework centered on specification-expanding reforms, stronger incentives for confirmatory research, and meta-analysis. This approach equips sociologists to assess the repeatability of findings and build a more cumulative discipline.

articles.title: Prediction-Based Adaptive Designs for Reducing Wave Nonresponse Rates and Bias in Panel Surveys
articles.authors: John Collins, Saskia Bartholomäus, Tobias Gummer, Bernd Weiß, Christoph Kern
articles.abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based nonresponse prediction in panel surveys enables selective interventions. However, the optimal use of ML predictions in Adaptive Survey Design (ASD) remains uncertain. We propose a method that integrates field experiment results on incentives, questionnaire length, and questionnaire content with ML-based propensity models to simulate ASD strategies ex-post with minimal assumptions. Using German panel data, we show that treating 15 percent of panelists, selected through ML-based predictions and R-indicator analysis, with increased cash incentives or a survey module on the respondents’ preferred topic can reduce nonresponse rates by up to 2 percentage points. These strategies also reduced bias in selected variables. We present our method as a framework for survey researchers to evaluate the expected outcomes of multiple ASD regimes simultaneously in a realistic setting. The framework helps identify both the criteria for allocating treatments to specific participant groups and the most effective modifications to the survey protocol.

articles.title: Dynamics of Local Clustering in Temporal Social Networks
articles.authors: Cheng Wang, Omar Lizardo, David S. Hachen
articles.abstract: While the local clustering coefficient is central to network analysis, it is typically treated as a static property. We introduce delta clustering to quantify changes in an individual's local clustering across adjacent time points in undirected networks. To address structural constraints, we develop a density-based decomposition expressing clustering as a weighted combination of subgraph-specific densities, clarifying how ego-network size and composition bound clustering change. We identify six triadic components distinguishing reconfiguration among persisting contacts from the integration and loss of ties. Using high-resolution university communication networks, we estimate fixed effects models accounting for network size interactions. Variation in delta clustering is driven primarily by density changes among persisting contacts, followed by the integration of new contacts, with magnitudes conditioned by ego-network size and baseline density. We further demonstrate the measure's explanatory power by linking daily clustering changes to individual behavioral outcomes. These results establish delta clustering as a size-aware, temporally grounded measure of local structural change in dynamic social networks.

articles.title: How Model Choice and Memory Shape Preference Consistency in Large Language Models
articles.abstract: When a language model answers a sequence of questions, researchers report the model and temperature but rarely what or how it was told about its own earlier answers. I show that this underreported setting behaves as a mode effect. Testing four large language model (LLM) families with revealed preference theory (GARP) across moral, economic, and social tasks ( N = 5,926 ), I find that how prior choices re-enter the prompt, the memory condition , moves the share of internally consistent subjects by up to 48 percentage points, mostly where that share starts lowest. Memory also influences which preferences the models express and, in a silicon-sampling extension, it brings the answers closer to the human distribution. Nonetheless, gains in consistency and surface fidelity do not necessarily translate into representativeness: a consistent, human-looking model may not represent any human population. For LLMs as social-science instruments, this study offers promise, caution, and a method for testing the stability of sequential outputs.

articles.title: Trends and Heterogeneity in Interracial Marriage in the United States, 1960 to 2023
articles.abstract: Although scholars recognize that interracial marriage in the United States has grown exponentially since the 1960s, our understanding of this trend for specific racial pairings is piecemeal and thin, because of issues with data comparability and lack of information on marriage timing between 1980 and 2007. In this study, the author uses log-linear models of census and American Community Survey data to analyze trends in interracial marriage from 1960 to 2023 across major single-race groups, as well as important subgroups and large multiracial groups. Weights are applied to match the joint age distribution of currently married partners to the age distribution of newlyweds in the same time period. Although the overall trend is one of exponential increase, important heterogeneity is visible when examining particular racial pairings or subgroups. Most notably, the likelihood of interracial marriage for East/Southeast Asian and American Indian/Alaska Native spouses plateaued by the end of the twentieth century and has not continued to grow. On the other hand, the likelihood of interracial marriage for Black spouses, although far lower than for any other group at the start of the period, has increased more rapidly than any other group. Overall, these results indicate an ongoing transformation of group boundaries.
